hints: Count carbons carefully, remembering the carbon in the CN group counts as one of the four carbons in butanenitrile.
Recall that reacting a halogenoalkane with cyanide ion replaces Br with CN and so adds exactly one extra carbon to the chain.
Check which starting material has three carbons and which reagent supplies CN, then match that to the product with four carbons.
walkthrough:
**Count the carbons in the target**

Look at butanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$. It has four carbons in total.

Three are in the propyl chain, one is in the $\text{CN}$ group:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} = 3 + 1 = 4 \text{ carbons}$$

**Recall the two ways to make a nitrile group**

There are two key routes you must separate. Substitution of a halogenoalkane with cyanide adds one carbon. Addition of $\text{HCN}$ to a carbonyl makes a hydroxynitrile, not a simple nitrile.

Substitution route:
$$\text{R-Br} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{R-CN} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Apply the carbon rule to choose the start**

Because the $\text{CN}$ carbon is new, the starting halogenoalkane must have one carbon fewer than the product. For a 4-carbon nitrile, you need a 3-carbon halogenoalkane.

That is 1-bromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, heated with $\text{KCN}$ in ethanol:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{Br}^-$$

options.A: Ammonia with a halogenoalkane gives an amine by nucleophilic substitution, not a nitrile. 1-bromobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, with $\text{NH}_3$ would give butylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. This is the amine trap.
options.B: This is correct. 1-bromopropane has three carbons. Cyanide ion, $\text{CN}^-$, acts as a nucleophile and replaces bromide. The new C-C bond adds the fourth carbon to give butanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$. Heating in ethanol favours substitution.
options.C: Propanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, is an aldehyde. With $\text{HCN}$ and $\text{KCN}$ catalyst it undergoes nucleophilic addition to give a hydroxynitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CN}$, not butanenitrile. Students who forget the OH group choose this.
options.D: Propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, is a ketone. With $\text{HCN}$ it also gives a hydroxynitrile, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(OH)CN}$. This is 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile, a branched hydroxynitrile, not the straight chain butanenitrile.
